canonical_title: EduQuest: RPG-Based Learning Management and Quiz Game Platform
abstract: EduQuest is a gamified educational web platform designed to improve student engagement in learning through role-playing game (RPG) mechanics. The system combines quiz-based assessment with interactive gameplay, where students answer questions, fight bosses, gain experience points (XP), level up, and collect items. The system supports three user roles: student, teacher, and admin. Teachers can create and manage courses, build quiz quests manually or by CSV import, and monitor student performance. Students can join classes through OTP-based enrollment, complete quests, and track their own growth through profile and inventory systems. Admin users oversee platform operations, including course approval, user management, and report resolution. EduQuest is implemented using React and Phaser for the frontend experience, Node.js/Express for backend services, and MongoDB for persistent storage. Security measures include JWT authentication, password hashing with bcrypt, and rate limiting for sensitive endpoints.

abstract: Sportify is an AI-supported fitness application developed to address three persistent issues in personal wellness management: fragmented tracking tools, limited personalized guidance, and declining user motivation. The proposed system integrates workout tracking, calorie logging, conversational AI support, and a rule-based achievement system within a single mobile platform. By combining practical self-monitoring functions with a user-friendly multilingual interface, the project aims to help users manage fitness goals more consistently and with less cognitive effort. The system adopts a mobile-first architecture using React Native and Expo for the frontend, Node.js and Express for backend services, Supabase for cloud data storage, JSON Web Token for authentication, and HuggingFace services for natural-language interaction. As a senior project prototype, Sportify demonstrates the feasibility of integrating intelligent assistance and gamification into a practical health application. Although the system still relies on manual data entry and has not yet undergone large-scale user evaluation, it provides a strong foundation for future enhancements such as wearable integration, richer analytics, and more advanced recommendation logic.

canonical_title: Rail Shooter Game With Computer Vision
abstract: This project introduces a 3D motion-controlled Rail Shooter Game where players can control the game with their body and hands instead of using traditional devices such as keyboards and mice or external controllers. Developed using the Unity Game Engine and integrated with the MediaPipe Unity Plugin, the system detects real-time body pose via a standard PC webcam, which is then translated into the game to move, aim, and shoot. The core technology stack consists of Unity (C#) for rendering and gameplay logic, and Google's MediaPipe Pose (BlazePose) model for 33-point anatomical landmark detection, bridged through a native C++ interop layer to avoid the latency penalties of network socket communication. The game employs a dual-stream control architecture: the player’s nose landmark (index 0) drives spatial navigation of an in-game spaceship, while wrist landmarks (indices 15 and 16) independently control two aiming crosshairs with an automatic firing system. The system follows a component-based architecture, consistent with Unity’s compound game engine design, where focused MonoBehaviour scripts communicate through C# static events, serialized Inspector references, and singleton services. Multiple layers of smoothing, including Vector3.SmoothDamp, exponential moving averages, velocity dead zones, and DOTween easing, are applied to filter natural human jitter from the tracking data without introducing excessive input lag. The project aims to make motion-controlled gaming, typically associated with expensive VR headsets or specialized controllers like the Nintendo Wii and the Nintendo Switch, more accessible to anyone with a basic computer setup. User evaluation at the Senior Project Exhibition with 42 participants yielded an average experience rating of 8.98 out of 10, with 97.6% of players expressing willingness to play again. The system achieved a stable 60 FPS during active gameplay with sub-100ms input latency, demonstrating that computer vision algorithms can be optimized for real-time, standalone PC gaming applications.
